prize_parts.citation: For discoveries of the incretin hormone GLP-1 and its active form, which established the physiological basis for GLP-1-based therapies for diabetes and obesity

statement.case_for: All six of us placed B017 first, but unanimity is not the argument. The scientific case is that it is one of the few chains that runs from hormone physiology (Holst on secretion and action in humans), through proglucagon processing and receptor biology (Drucker), to identification of the bioactive GLP-1(7-36) peptide (Mojsov), and on to therapies with randomized outcome evidence in glycaemia, weight, cardiovascular and renal endpoints. The discovery is original, mechanistically clear, independently confirmed for decades, and the scale of its effect on medicine is very large. Framing the citation around the physiological discovery of the incretin and its active form keeps the prize within physiology or medicine and avoids a pure drug-development award.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Priority for the active peptide form and the insulinotropic role is disputed, Habener and other early investigators are not among the credited names, and omitting Knudsen leaves out the person who designed the long-acting agonists that produced most of the clinical impact. A three-person limit forces a choice between a physiology prize and a physiology-plus-pharmaceutical prize, and either choice leaves a visible gap. I accept that gap, but it should be stated openly rather than treated as settled.

responses.point: Linnarsson proposed Drucker, Holst and Knudsen, arguing that the design of liraglutide and semaglutide is what turned the physiology into a transformative drug class, while Mojsov's role is contested.
responses.response: I take the point that Knudsen's acylation chemistry is what made once-daily and once-weekly dosing possible, and that without it the clinical impact would be much smaller. I still disagree on the third seat. The prize category rewards a discovery, and the identification of the active GLP-1 peptide is a discovery that the drug work depends on, whereas Knudsen's contribution is an engineering step on top of it. If the committee prefers to honour the drug design, I would want that argued explicitly as a different achievement and not folded in by default. I also accept that the dispute over Mojsov's priority is real and I have not verified it, so I regard her inclusion as the weaker of the three names.

responses.point: Wahren-Herlenius also chose Knudsen alongside Drucker and Holst and ranked TNF blockade (B018) third, valuing anti-cytokine therapy as a transformation of inflammatory disease care, while stressing that attribution in B017 is contested.
responses.response: I agree with her that attribution in B017 is contested and that we should not pretend otherwise. On B018, I see a clean two-person configuration, but the work is mainly translational: the antibody engineering and TNF biology sit outside Feldmann and Maini. I would not put it above B017, and I rank it lower than she does, although I do not dispute the clinical impact. Where we differ is the weight on Knudsen. I would hold the third seat for peptide identification, and I think the 'timely, mature' argument we both make does not depend on who holds that seat.

responses.point: El-Manira proposed Drucker, Holst and Mojsov for B017, leaving out Knudsen as pharmaceutical development, and ranked the unfolded protein response (B022) and optogenetics (B049) in his top four.
responses.response: We converge on the B017 trio and on the reasoning for it. I would qualify his optogenetics choice of Bamberg, Nagel and Deisseroth. Omitting Hegemann and Boyden is hard to defend scientifically, since the channelrhodopsin work and its neuronal deployment are shared among at least five or six people. That crowding is the reason I keep B049 below the clinically proven candidates. His point that the work is a research tool as much as a physiological discovery also lowers its rank for me. I take the unfolded protein response as a clean two-person case, but its clinical translation is still emerging, so I do not think it should displace a prize with proven human impact.

responses.point: Svenningsson ranked B017 first with the same trio, then placed imatinib (B024) second and HPV vaccines (B016) third, noting the priority and patent dispute between Frazer and Zhou and the earlier 2008 HPV prize.
responses.response: I agree on B017 and on the Frazer and Zhou issue. For B016 the 2008 prize covered the HPV-cancer link, but the vaccine is a separate and mechanistically clean achievement, so I do not think the earlier prize rules it out. The unresolved priority question is the real risk, and Zhou's death means the living-names constraint cannot repair it. On B024, I rank it a little lower than he does. The Philadelphia chromosome and BCR-ABL discoveries sit outside the credited names, and the award would honour drug development, though I do not doubt its paradigm-setting role. I would keep B024 as an alternative, not as a second part, because a split prize would force the B017 union below the three names I think it needs.

responses.point: Perlmann ranked the same B017 trio first, and placed imatinib (B024) third and cGAS-STING (B042) fourth, questioning whether a drug-development prize fits the committee's preference for fundamental discovery.
responses.response: His question about fit is the right one, and it applies to B017 too, which is why I want the citation to rest on the incretin discovery and not on the drugs. I would answer it differently for B024: imatinib's value is the proof of principle for targeted therapy, but the foundational lesion discovery lies elsewhere, so it fits the committee's stated preference less well than B017. On B042 I share his view that the mechanism is original and well confirmed, but that therapeutic translation is unproven, so I leave it off my preferred configuration.

uncertainties: Priority for identifying the active GLP-1 peptide form and its insulinotropic role (Mojsov, Habener and others) is disputed, and I have not verified it from the supplied evidence.
Whether the third seat should go to peptide identification (Mojsov) or to long-acting agonist design (Knudsen).
Whether CAR-T (B006) would be better as a single-achievement prize if the committee does not settle B017, given that Eshhar is outside the credited names.
statement.conflict_note: I have co-authored with Sten Linnarsson (eight joint works per the profile) and with Jonas Frisén, and I am at Karolinska Institutet. None of the shortlisted candidates involves them or my own work, and no specific conflict with any shortlisted ballot ID is apparent from the provided profile. Shared affiliation alone does not establish a conflict.
